individual_reviews.label: reviewer_1

review.Summary: The paper proposes InSTA, a fully automated pipeline for generating web-navigation training data at internet scale without human annotations. It consists of three stages: a frozen LLM task proposer that annotates 150k safe websites (from the top 1M Common Crawl hosts) with agentic tasks via a feedback loop; LLM agents that execute these tasks in a virtual browser to produce trajectories; and an LLM judge that filters successful trajectories. The authors evaluate the safety filter (up to 97% accuracy), judge accuracy (up to 82.6%), and train Qwen 3 1.7B agents on the generated data, achieving 56.9% success on a held-out InSTA test set and competitive zero-shot transfer to WebVoyager, while being much smaller than frontier models. Code, models, and data are released.
Strengths: The paper tackles an important problem—reducing human annotation burden for web-agent training—and proposes a fully automated, scalable pipeline with task proposer, agent, and judge components; the scale of 150k sites is a clear advance over existing datasets limited to a few hundred sites.

Extensive empirical validation of pipeline components: safety filter accuracy up to 97%, judge accuracy up to 82.6%, and human verification of 300 tasks; these evaluations, while limited, go beyond what many synthetic-data papers report.

Training Qwen 3 1.7B on filtered InSTA data yields strong results: 56.9% success on the held-out InSTA set, outperforming the 235B data-collection policy, and zero-shot transfer to WebVoyager; this demonstrates the practical value of the generated data.
The paper provides a thoughtful discussion of safety, PII removal, web interaction limits, and broader impacts, and releases code, models, and data to facilitate reproducibility and future research.
The cost analysis (e.g., ~$1.5k for Llama 3.1 70B serving vs. ~$20k+ API costs) makes a compelling case for accessible large-scale data generation.
Weaknesses: Evaluation relies heavily on LLM judges: the main success rate (56.9%) is measured by a Qwen 3 235B judge, and human verification is limited to 100 trajectories for judge accuracy; no human evaluation of the final trained agent is reported, so the true task-completion rate remains uncertain.

The held-out InSTA test set is drawn from the same distribution as the training data (same task proposer and similar websites), so the reported gains may partly reflect overfitting to the pipeline's task distribution; stronger evidence would require human-annotated evaluation or more diverse external benchmarks.

There are inconsistencies and missing experimental details: e.g., Section 5.2 says a fine-tuned Qwen3 1.7B was the data-collection agent, while Section 6.1 says a Qwen 3 235B policy collected trajectories; exact WebVoyager success numbers and error bars are not provided; the role of screenshots in training a text-only model is unclear.

The safety filter and reliability experiments use small, hand-picked sets (100 sites and 300 tasks), which may not reflect the diversity of the full 150k corpus; the 3% safety-filter error rate could still expose agents to harmful content at scale.

The paper does not compare against other automatic data-generation methods (e.g., PAE, Synatra, NNetNav) under matched conditions, making it difficult to isolate the contribution of specific design choices like the feedback loop and judge filtering.
Questions: How were the 100 trajectories for judge verification selected, and what was the inter-annotator agreement among the human workers? Is the 82.6% judge accuracy computed on the same distribution as the test set used for the 56.9% success rate?
What is the human-verified success rate on a sample of the 3,000-site InSTA test set? How does the judge's 82.6% accuracy affect the confidence interval of the reported 56.9%?

Can the authors clarify which policy was used for the large-scale 150k trajectory collection and which for the 20k training trajectories in Section 6.1? Why is a fine-tuned 1.7B model used as the data-collection agent in one place and Qwen 3 235B in another?
Are the websites in the WebVoyager benchmark guaranteed to be absent from the Common Crawl pages used for training? How was this verified given that web content and site structures change over time?
What are the exact WebVoyager success rates (with standard deviations) for the trained Qwen 3 1.7B and the frontier baselines under each judge? Were the differences statistically significant?
How many of the 2.2M screenshots were actually used in training? If the model is text-only, what information do screenshots provide beyond the Markdown representation?
Limitations: LLM judge errors (up to 17.4% misclassification) can propagate into training data and final performance estimates, and the confidence calibration may not hold for out-of-distribution sites or tasks.
The task proposer excludes social media, forums, account-required sites, and tasks that modify web state, so the resulting agents may not generalize to those important real-world scenarios.

Automated web scraping at internet scale may violate website terms of service or local laws regarding crawling and data usage; the paper limits interaction rate but does not address legal compliance mechanisms beyond robots.txt-inspired suggestions.
The pipeline inherits biases and safety issues from the LLMs used for task generation, judging, and data filtering; harmful content that evades the filter could be included in released data.
No experiments with multimodal tasks (despite collecting screenshots) or with reinforcement learning, so the full promise of the dynamic flywheel is not yet demonstrated.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_2

review.Summary: The paper presents InSTA, a fully automated pipeline for curating internet-scale web-agent training data. It uses an LLM task proposer to generate tasks for 150k websites, an LLM agent to produce trajectories, and an LLM judge to filter successful data. The authors train Qwen 3 1.7B agents on this data and report competitive performance against much larger models, including zero-shot transfer to WebVoyager, WebLINX, and Mind2Web, and release code/model/data.
Strengths: The InSTA pipeline removes the need for human annotations in web-agent data collection and scales to 150k live websites, a much larger and more diverse task set than prior work.
The released dataset (150k tasks, 2.2M screenshots and action traces) and trained models are likely useful to the community.
The paper provides evidence that judge-filtered data leads to better scaling: the 1.7B model improves with more data and outperforms the 235B data-collection policy on the held-out test.
Transfer results to WebVoyager and to static benchmarks like Mind2Web/WebLINX are promising and constitute a stronger generalization test than training and testing on the same sites.
The safety filter is evaluated on a human-labeled set and shows high accuracy/recall, and the appendix contains thoughtful discussion of limitations and safeguards.
Weaknesses: The central evaluation metric is an LLM judge with only 82.6% accuracy on 100 human-annotated trajectories; no human evaluation is provided for the final claims of matching/surpassing frontier LLMs, so the headline numbers may reflect judge bias or noise.
Results lack error bars, confidence intervals, and multiple runs; with a 3,000-task test set and judge accuracy <85%, the differences reported could be within noise.

The held-out test set is generated by the same task proposer and judged by the same LLM family used to filter training data, creating a distribution shift that favors models trained on InSTA; zero-shot transfer to WebVoyager mitigates but does not eliminate this concern.

No comparisons are made to existing fine-tuned small web agents (e.g., PAE, WebVoyager-trained models) under identical conditions, so it is unclear whether the gains are from the pipeline itself or from the base model/training setup.
Safety and reliability evaluations are based on only 100 sites and 300 tasks, which is a small sample relative to 150k; the paper does not report false-negative rates on the full set.

The pipeline interacts with 150k live websites without explicit discussion of robots.txt compliance or obtaining consent from website owners; even with limited actions, this raises ethical and legal concerns.
Questions: What are the exact success rates and confidence intervals for all compared models (Qwen 3 235B, Llama 4 Maverick, Gemini 2.5 Flash, and the trained 1.7B models) on the held-out test set, and how many evaluator trajectories were used?
Would the main conclusions change if the held-out test set were evaluated by human annotators or by a judge that was not involved in data filtering?
How exactly was train-test overlap prevented for the 150k sites and the WebVoyager/Mind2Web/WebLINX splits? Please provide automated overlap checks and the percentage of overlapping URLs.
Does the judge's 82.6% accuracy on 100 trajectories hold across task categories and website popularity ranges, and what is the inter-judge agreement on the final test set?
What is the success rate of the Qwen 3 235B data-collection policy on the 20k training trajectories, and is the 56.9% of the 1.7B model measured on the same tasks with the same judge?
Did the authors consider respecting robots.txt or other website access policies, and what is the legal/ethical basis for automatically generating tasks and acting on 150k live sites?
Limitations: Evaluation relies on LLM judges; judge accuracy is only 82.6% on 100 examples.
Human validation sets are small (100 sites, 300 tasks), limiting confidence in safety and reliability estimates.
The task distribution is limited by the Playwright API and the task proposer's prompt; some categories are infeasible or require capabilities outside the action space.
PII and copyrighted content are only partially mitigated by prompt instructions and scrubadub; the paper acknowledges residual risk.
The pipeline is not truly internet-scale: it starts with the top 1M sites and filters to 150k, which is still a small fraction of the web.
Only textual tasks and observations are used in training, despite the collection of multimodal screenshots.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_3

review.Summary: The paper introduces InSTA, an automatic pipeline for curating large-scale web navigation training data without human annotations. The pipeline consists of three stages: an LLM task proposer annotates 150k websites with agentic tasks (and filters unsafe sites), LLM agents execute tasks to produce trajectories, and an LLM judge filters successful trajectories. The authors release the code, models, and data. They train Qwen 3 1.7B agents on this data and report a 56.9% success rate on a held-out test set, outperforming the Qwen 3 235B data collection policy and Llama 4 Maverick, and reaching 94.7% of Gemini 2.5 Flash's performance. They also show zero-shot transfer to WebVoyager and improvements on WebLINX and Mind2Web when mixing with human data.
Strengths: Novel and ambitious pipeline that automatically generates web navigation data at a scale far exceeding prior human-annotated datasets (150k sites vs. hundreds), directly addressing a key bottleneck in agent training.
Strong empirical demonstration that a small 1.7B model trained on this automatically curated data can match or approach frontier LLMs as web agents, with a 235x size reduction.
The paper emphasizes and implements a clean train-test split (e.g., zero-shot transfer to WebVoyager without any WebVoyager data), avoiding a common pitfall in prior work.
The release of code, models, and the official HuggingFace dataset is a valuable contribution to the community and should facilitate reproducibility and further research.
The analysis of the judge's confidence as a calibration signal (accuracy up to 93.1% for high-confidence predictions) is insightful and practically useful for data filtering.
Weaknesses: The primary evaluation relies on LLM judges rather than human verification, and the judge's accuracy is only 82.6% (GPT-4o) on a small set of 100 human-annotated trajectories. This casts uncertainty on the true success rates and the validity of comparing agents judged by the same (or similar) models.

The safety filter evaluation is limited to 100 curated websites (50 unsafe). This is a very small sample to justify the claim of 97% accuracy, and the false negative rate on the full 1M site crawl is not characterized.

There is a potential inconsistency in the data collection description: Section 5.2 says 150k trajectories were collected using a fine-tuned Qwen3 1.7B as the agent, while Section 6.1 says 20k trajectories were collected with a Qwen 3 235B policy. The relationship between these two datasets and why two different policies were used is unclear.

The paper does not compare against other automatic data-generation pipelines (e.g., PAE, NNetNav) or against agents trained on similarly sized human data, making it difficult to isolate the contribution of the proposed pipeline relative to existing methods.

The task proposer is instructed to avoid tasks involving accounts, transactions, or social media, which limits the diversity of tasks and may not reflect a truly 'internet-scale' agent environment. The paper acknowledges this but doesn't explore the impact.

The WebVoyager evaluation uses LLM judges to determine success, but WebVoyager's original protocol uses human evaluation. The paper does not provide human-verified success rates, so the reported 'matching frontier LLMs' may not hold under human evaluation.
Questions: How do you ensure that the LLM judge's success predictions align with human judgments beyond the 100 trajectory sample? Have you measured inter-annotator agreement or correlation with human success rates on WebVoyager?

What is the exact relationship between the 20k trajectories collected with the Qwen 3 235B policy in Section 6.1 and the 150k trajectories collected with a fine-tuned Qwen3 1.7B in Section 5.2? Why are these policies different, and how does this affect the conclusions about data scaling?

How did you verify that the top 1M Common Crawl sites have no overlap with the WebVoyager, Mind2Web, or WebLINX test websites? Could there be indirect contamination through shared content or subdomains?
The judge accuracy is 82.6% on a small human-labeled set. What is the human agreement on these 100 trajectories? Is the judge's error rate heterogeneous across task categories or websites?

Could the observed improvement from judge-filtered data be partly an artifact of the judge being the same Qwen 3 235B used to generate the trajectories? Have you compared filtering by a different judge (e.g., Gemini 2.5 Flash) to rule out self-bias?

What is the rate of tasks generated that are infeasible due to Playwright API limitations (e.g., downloads, file openings, complex multi-step interactions)? The paper mentions these in Figure 15, but not a quantified fraction.
Limitations: Evaluation relies heavily on LLM judges, which are imperfect and may be biased toward their own generation styles; the human validation set is small (100 trajectories).
Safety filtering is tested on only 100 sites, and the paper does not report the number of unsafe sites actually found in the 1M-site crawl or the precision/recall on that distribution.
The pipeline is not fully 'dynamic' in practice: it uses a single round of task generation and does not continuously update as websites change, despite claiming to unlock a dynamic environment.
The generated tasks are restricted to passive interactions (no purchases, no account creation), which limits the scope of tasks and may not generalize to important real-world agent applications.
The cost analysis assumes fixed token counts and does not account for retries, parsing failures, or the cost of the task proposer phase; actual costs may be higher.

Potential negative societal impacts: agents interacting with live websites could disturb analytics and affect real users, and the release of scraped web data may include PII or copyrighted material despite scrubbing efforts.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_4

review.Summary: The paper introduces InSTA, an automatic pipeline for generating web-agent training data at internet scale without human annotations. It uses an LLM task proposer to annotate ~150k real websites with agentic tasks, LLM agents to complete these tasks and produce trajectories, and an LLM judge to filter successful trajectories. The authors train Qwen3-1.7B agents on the resulting data and report competitive performance with frontier LLMs on their own test set and zero-shot on WebVoyager, while releasing code, models, and data.
Strengths: The pipeline scales task annotation to 150k real websites from Common Crawl, far exceeding the scale of existing human-annotated web-agent datasets and demonstrating a practical path toward internet-scale agent training data.

The empirical result is striking: a 1.7B parameter model trained on generated trajectories outperforms the 235B data collection policy and reaches close to Gemini 2.5 Flash performance, suggesting the generated data is highly effective for small models.

The paper includes multiple evaluation angles: safety filtering accuracy, LLM judge accuracy and confidence calibration, human reliability checks, zero-shot transfer to WebVoyager, and integration with Mind2Web/WebLINX, which strengthens the evidence for the pipeline's utility.
The observation that LLM judge confidence correlates with accuracy (up to 93.1% at full confidence) is practically useful for scalable and selective evaluation.
The release of code, models, and datasets supports reproducibility and community adoption, and the cost analysis provides a concrete estimate of the resources required.

review.Summary: The paper introduces InSTA, an automated pipeline for generating large-scale web navigation training data without human annotations. The pipeline uses an LLM task proposer to annotate 150k websites with agentic tasks while filtering unsafe content, LLM agents to complete these tasks and produce trajectories, and an LLM judge to score and filter successful trajectories. The authors train Qwen 3 1.7B agents on this data and report a 56.9% success rate on a held-out test set, claiming competitiveness with frontier LLMs such as Gemini 2.5 Flash and zero-shot transfer to WebVoyager. The code, models, and dataset are planned for release.
Strengths: The pipeline scales to an unprecedented size (150k websites, 2.2M screenshots and reasoning traces) and is designed to be fully automated, which could significantly reduce the dependence on human annotations for web agent training.

The experimental results show that a small 1.7B parameter model can be trained to outperform much larger models (Qwen 3 235B, Llama 4 Maverick) on the authors' test set, suggesting the generated data is effective for distillation.
The authors provide a detailed cost analysis and release pipeline components, which could make large-scale agent data collection accessible to academic labs with limited budgets.
Weaknesses: The primary evaluation relies on an LLM judge that is also used to filter training data, creating a self-referential bias; the judge is validated on only 100 human-annotated trajectories (82.6% accuracy), and no human evaluation is reported for the final test set success rates.

The test set consists of tasks generated by the same task proposer distribution used for training, and the claimed transfer to WebVoyager is evaluated using LLM judges rather than human evaluation, which may overstate real-world generalization.

The paper omits many technical details due to extensive redactions (e.g., exact prompts, hyperparameter tables, lists of unsafe websites), making reproduction difficult and limiting the paper's self-containedness.

The claim of a 'dynamic internet-scale environment' is overstated: the pipeline collects a static one-time snapshot of tasks and trajectories, with no repeated interaction or evolving task distribution, so it is essentially a large static dataset.

The safety filter evaluation is based on only 100 hand-picked websites, which is insufficient to demonstrate robustness across the diverse and harmful content on the internet; precision and recall may degrade significantly at scale.

The comparison to frontier LLMs is performed on the authors' own test set with an LLM judge, and no direct comparison to existing agent training pipelines (e.g., PAE or ScribeAgent) is provided on a common benchmark under the same evaluation protocol.
Questions: Who are the human annotators for the judge accuracy and reliability experiments, and is inter-annotator agreement reported?
How do the reported success rates change when evaluated by a different LLM judge (e.g., GPT-4o or Gemini) or by humans on a random subset of the test set?
Could the LLM judge exhibit systematic bias toward the fine-tuned Qwen 3 1.7B agent because of the shared Qwen 3 backbone used for both data collection and judging?
What is the PageRank distribution of the 150k retained sites, and how does task difficulty or success rate vary with PageRank?
Have you compared your training data against existing datasets (e.g., PAE outputs or ScribeAgent data) using the same base model and evaluation protocol on WebVoyager?
Why are screenshots collected but not used in training or evaluation, given the claim of a multimodal reasoning dataset?
Limitations: The evaluation is dominated by LLM-based judges with only small-scale human validation, leaving the reported success rates uncertain.
The safety filter is tested on only 100 curated websites, and its precision/recall on the full internet-scale distribution is unknown; subtle harmful or illegal tasks may slip through.
Data collection involves live website interaction; the paper limits engagement but does not fully assess risks to third-party sites or the potential for unintended consequences.
The released dataset may still contain copyrighted or personally identifiable information despite scrubbing, and no residual PII analysis is provided.
The trained agents operate on a text-only Markdown representation and do not use the collected screenshots, which limits the claimed multimodal value of the dataset.

review.Summary: The paper introduces InSTA, a fully automated pipeline for generating web-navigation training data at internet scale without human annotations. It consists of an LLM task proposer that annotates ~150k safe websites with agentic tasks, LLM agents that execute these tasks in a shared virtual browser, and an LLM judge that filters successful trajectories. The authors train Qwen3-1.7B agents on the resulting data and report a 56.9% success rate on a held-out InSTA test set, outperforming the 235B data-collection policy and approaching Gemini 2.5 Flash, with zero-shot transfer to WebVoyager. Code, models, and data are released.
Strengths: Scales web-agent training data generation to 150k live websites, far exceeding prior human-annotated datasets and demonstrating a practical path toward internet-scale data.

A small 1.7B model trained on automatically generated data outperforms much larger models on the authors' test set and transfers zero-shot to WebVoyager, highlighting the data's value for distillation.

The pipeline is fully automated and includes safety filtering, task proposal, trajectory collection, and judge-based filtering, with component-wise evaluations on safety, judge accuracy, and reliability.
The paper provides a thoughtful cost analysis and releases code, models, and the dataset, supporting reproducibility and further community research.
The finding that LLM judge confidence correlates with accuracy is practically useful for scalable selective evaluation.
Weaknesses: The primary evaluation relies on an LLM judge that is the same model family used for data generation and filtering, and it is validated on only 100 human-annotated trajectories (82.6% accuracy). No human evaluation of the final trained agent is reported, so absolute success rates remain uncertain.

The held-out InSTA test set is generated by the same task proposer and judged by the same LLM family used to filter training data, creating a distribution shift that favors models trained on InSTA; transfer to WebVoyager mitigates but does not eliminate this concern.

There are inconsistencies in the data collection description: Section 5.2 says a fine-tuned Qwen3-1.7B collected 150k trajectories, while Section 6.1 uses 20k trajectories from a Qwen3-235B policy; the relationship between these datasets and which drives the reported gains is unclear.

Safety and reliability evaluations are based on small hand-picked samples (100 sites for safety, ~300 tasks for reliability), giving wide error bars; the false-negative rate on the full 1M-site crawl is not characterized.

No controlled comparison is made against other automatic data-generation pipelines (e.g., PAE, NNetNav) or against agents trained on similarly scaled human or synthetic data, making it difficult to isolate the contribution of specific design choices.
Several implementation details are redacted (exact prompts, hyperparameters, unsafe-site lists), limiting reproducibility from the submission itself.
Questions: What is the human-verified success rate of the final Qwen3-1.7B agent on a random sample of held-out tasks, rather than judge-assigned scores?
How do the 150k trajectories collected with the fine-tuned Qwen3-1.7B in Section 5.2 relate to the 20k Qwen3-235B trajectories in Section 6.1, and which dataset produces the best final agent?
How was the 100-site safety test constructed, and what are confidence intervals for the reported accuracy, precision, and recall?

Can the authors provide overlap statistics showing that the training sites do not overlap with WebVoyager/Mind2Web/WebLINX test websites, considering potential content overlap beyond exact URL matches?
Would the main conclusions change if the held-out test set were evaluated by a judge that was not involved in data filtering or by human annotators on a larger sample?
What are the exact WebVoyager success rates with standard deviations for all compared models, and were the differences statistically significant?
Limitations: The evaluation is dominated by LLM judges with only small-scale human validation, and judge errors (up to 17.4%) propagate into both training-data filtering and final performance estimates.
The safety filter is tested on only 100 curated websites, so its precision/recall on the full internet-scale distribution is unknown; harmful or illegal tasks may slip through.
The pipeline excludes account-required, social media, transactional, and state-modifying tasks, limiting the diversity of real-world web interactions.
Automated interaction with 150k live websites raises legal and ethical concerns regarding robots.txt compliance, website terms of service, and potential disturbance to live services.
The dataset may still contain PII or copyrighted content despite scrubbing, and no residual PII analysis is provided.
Despite collecting 2.2M screenshots, the trained model is text-only, so the multimodal value of the dataset is not demonstrated.
